description: Learn how Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) and Clickjacking work, and how to defend using Anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, and X-Frame-Options.

slides.title: Introduction to CSRF
slides.content:
# Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) 🎭

**Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)** (also known as "one-click attack" or "session riding") is an attack where a malicious website tricks a victim's web browser into performing unauthorized actions on a trusted site where the user is currently authenticated.

## The Core Vulnerability Principle

Web browsers automatically include authentication cookies with **every HTTP request** to a domain, regardless of which website originated the request!

If an application assumes that any request carrying a valid cookie was intentionally submitted by the user, it is vulnerable to CSRF.

slides.title: How CSRF Works: A Concrete Scenario
slides.content: # Step-by-Step CSRF Attack Mechanics ⚙️ Imagine Alice is logged into her bank account at `bank.com`. 1. Alice logs in; `bank.com` sets a session cookie in her browser. 2. Without logging out, Alice visits `evil-site.com` in another browser tab. 3. `evil-site.com` contains a hidden image or form: ```html_not ``` 4. Alice's browser attempts to download the "image", making an HTTP GET request to `bank.com`. 5. The browser **automatically attaches Alice's session cookie**! 6. `bank.com` verifies the valid cookie and transfers $10,000 to the attacker without Alice ever knowing!

slides.title: CSRF via HTTP POST Forms
slides.content:
# CSRF via Hidden Auto-Submitting POST Forms 📝 Even if bank transfers require an HTTP POST request, attackers can bypass this with automated hidden forms: ```html_not

You won a free iPhone! Processing...

``` The moment Alice visits the page, JavaScript automatically submits the form across origins, and the browser attaches her credentials!

slides.title: Impact of CSRF Attacks
slides.content:
# The Real-World Impact of CSRF 💥

A successful CSRF attack can execute any state-changing action the victim is authorized to perform:

- 📧 **Email & Password Reset**: Changing the account's registered email address to an attacker-controlled address.
- 💸 **Financial Fraud**: Initiating wire transfers, making unauthorized purchases, adding fraudulent shipping addresses.
- 🔓 **Router Hijacking**: Exploiting home routers using default credentials to change DNS servers to malicious servers.
- 🛡️ **Privilege Escalation**: Forcing an authenticated administrator to create a new admin user.

slides.title: Primary Defense: Anti-CSRF Tokens
slides.content:
# Anti-CSRF Tokens: Synchronizer Token Pattern 🛡️

The industry gold standard for CSRF prevention is the **Synchronizer Token Pattern**.

## How It Works

1. When the user loads a form, the server generates a cryptographically random, unpredictable token tied to the user's current session.
2. The server embeds this token in the HTML form as a hidden input:
   ```html_not
   <form action="/transfer" method="POST">
     <input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="9a8f7c6e5b4a3d2e1f0e9d8c7b6a5">
     <input type="text" name="amount">
     <button type="submit">Transfer</button>
   </form>
   ```
3. When submitted, the server compares the submitted token against the session token. If they do not match or the token is missing, the request is rejected with `403 Forbidden`.

slides.title: Why Anti-CSRF Tokens Stop Attackers
slides.content:
# Why Attackers Cannot Forge Anti-CSRF Tokens 🚫

Remember the **Same-Origin Policy (SOP)**?

- An attacker hosting a form on `evil-site.com` can forge the POST request.
- However, because of SOP, `evil-site.com` **CANNOT read the HTML of `bank.com`**!
- Because the attacker cannot read the page, they cannot steal the secret `_csrf` token.
- Without the token, the server immediately denies the forged request.

slides.title: Modern Browser Defense: SameSite Cookie Attribute
slides.content:
# The Game Changer: `SameSite` Cookie Attribute 🍪

The `SameSite` cookie attribute allows web developers to control whether cookies are attached to cross-site requests.

## Three Values of SameSite

| Value | Cross-Site Navigations (`<a href>`) | Cross-Site POST Forms | Cross-Site Images/Frames |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SameSite=Strict` | ❌ Blocked | ❌ Blocked | ❌ Blocked |
| `SameSite=Lax` (Default) | ✅ Sent (Top-level GET only) | ❌ Blocked | ❌ Blocked |
| `SameSite=None` | ✅ Sent (Requires `Secure`) | ✅ Sent | ✅ Sent |

```http_not
Set-Cookie: sessionId=xyz123; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
```

slides.title: SameSite=Strict vs SameSite=Lax
slides.content:
# Strict vs Lax in Practice ⚖️

## `SameSite=Strict`

The cookie is **never** sent in any cross-site context. If a user clicks a link to `bank.com` from an external email or Google search, they will initially appear logged out until they click a link within `bank.com` itself.

- *Best for*: High-security dashboards, banking apps, administrative consoles.

## `SameSite=Lax` (Modern Browser Default)

Permits cookies on top-level incoming navigations (like clicking a link from Google search), but **blocks cookies on cross-site POST forms, iframes, and AJAX requests**.

- *Best for*: General consumer web applications.

slides.title: Double Submit Cookie Pattern
slides.content:
# The Double Submit Cookie Pattern 👯

What if your API servers are stateless and cannot store session tokens in a database or Redis cache?

## How Double Submit Works

1. When a user authenticates, the server generates a random token and sets it as a non-HttpOnly cookie: `Set-Cookie: csrf-token=random123`.
2. When submitting a request, frontend JavaScript reads `csrf-token` from the cookie and sends it as a custom header: `X-CSRF-Token: random123`.
3. The server compares the cookie value against the header value. If both match, the request is authentic.

> ⚠️ **Security Warning:** The Double Submit Cookie pattern must use HMAC cryptographic signing to prevent attackers from overwriting cookies via subdomain poisoning!

slides.title: Verifying Origin and Referer Headers
slides.content:
# Verifying Origin & Referer Headers 🧭

Modern browsers automatically send the `Origin` header with state-changing requests (`POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`).

```http_not
POST /api/transfer HTTP/1.1
Host: mybank.com
Origin: https://mybank.com
Referer: https://mybank.com/transfer-funds
```

## Server Verification Rule

The backend should verify that the `Origin` or `Referer` header matches the expected host:

```javascript_not
const origin = req.headers['origin'];
if (!origin || origin !== 'https://mybank.com') {
  return res.status(403).json({ error: 'Untrusted origin' });
}
```

slides.title: Clickjacking: The UI Redressing Attack
slides.content: # Clickjacking (UI Redressing) 🖱️ **Clickjacking** is a deceptive attack where an attacker embeds a legitimate website inside a transparent ` ```

slides.title: Defense: X-Frame-Options Header
slides.content:
# Defending Against Clickjacking: `X-Frame-Options` 🛡️

The `X-Frame-Options` HTTP response header tells the browser whether a page is allowed to be rendered within a `<frame>`, `<iframe>`, or `<object>`.

## Three Directives

1. **`DENY`**: Completely forbids any domain (including the site itself) from framing the page:
   ```http_not
   X-Frame-Options: DENY
   ```
2. **`SAMEORIGIN`**: Permits framing only if the parent frame is on the exact same origin:
   ```http_not
   X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
   ```
3. **`ALLOW-FROM uri`** *(Deprecated)*: Replaced by modern CSP.

slides.title: Modern Frame Defense: CSP frame-ancestors
Legacy Defense: Frame Busting Scripts
slides.content:
# Legacy Frame Busting Scripts 🪓

Before `X-Frame-Options` existed, developers wrote client-side JavaScript to detect and break out of iframes:

```javascript_not
// Classic Frame Buster
if (top.location !== self.location) {
  top.location = self.location; // Break out to top window
}
```

## Why Frame Busting Scripts Fail

Attackers can neutralize frame-busting scripts using the HTML5 `sandbox` attribute on the iframe (`<iframe sandbox="allow-forms allow-scripts">`), which prevents the child iframe from redirecting the top window.

**Conclusion:** Always rely on HTTP headers (`X-Frame-Options` & CSP), never on JavaScript frame busters!

slides.title: CSRF Defense in Modern Web Frameworks
slides.content:
# CSRF Protection in Modern Frameworks ⚙️

Most mature backend frameworks provide automated CSRF protection out of the box:

- **Django**: Auto-enables `CsrfViewMiddleware` and `{% csrf_token %}` tag.
- **Ruby on Rails**: `protect_from_forgery with: :exception`.
- **Express.js**: The `csurf` or `@dr.pogodin/csurf` middleware.
- **ASP.NET Core**: Automatic anti-forgery tokens on all HTML tag helpers.

> ⚠️ **Gotcha:** Do NOT disable CSRF middleware just to make testing with Postman easier!

slides.title: Summary: CSRF & Clickjacking
slides.content:
# CSRF & Clickjacking: Summary 📋

## Key Takeaways
- **CSRF**: Forces a user's browser to submit authenticated requests to a foreign server.
- **Anti-CSRF Tokens**: Unpredictable, unique tokens validated per session.
- **SameSite Cookies**: Set `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` to prevent ambient cookie attachment on cross-site requests.
- **Verify Origin**: Inspect `Origin` and `Referer` headers on state-changing requests.
- **Clickjacking**: Tricking users into clicking invisible iframes.
- **Frame Defense**: Use `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` and `CSP frame-ancestors 'self'`.
